claims.text: The initial (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy has a fine-grained, relatively homogeneous microstructure.
The initial alloy exhibits a large caloric effect.
The initial alloy has poor load-bearing integrity and tends to crack under mechanical loading.
Partial recrystallization annealing can create a heterogeneous mixture of nano-, ultrafine-, and micrometer-sized grains in the target alloy.
The annealing can be conducted without altering the order-disorder transition responsible for the caloric effect.
Partial recrystallization should be stopped before complete recrystallization produces a uniform grain size.
The resulting heterogeneous structure will contain abundant twin boundaries and grain boundaries.
Heterogeneous grain sizes promote internal load partitioning and internal-stress or back-stress hardening.
Twin formation contributes to strengthening and sustained strain hardening.
Load partitioning, back-stress hardening, and twinning will delay crack initiation and enhance ductility in the target alloy.
The target alloy's caloric response is driven by an atomic-scale order-disorder transition.
Changing grain-size heterogeneity while leaving the order-disorder transition unchanged will preserve caloric performance.
Relative to the unchanged alloy, the annealed alloy will have greater tensile strength and ductility.
Relative to the unchanged alloy, the annealed alloy will have greater toughness and reduced crack propagation.
The annealed alloy will retain a similar caloric entropy change or adiabatic temperature change under applied fields.
The treatment is applicable over refrigeration operating temperatures and under the magnetic or pressure fields currently used to trigger the caloric response.
The proposed validity range is limited to mechanical loading conditions in which cracking is the critical failure mode and to processing that does not alter the order-disorder transition.

A controlled comparison of conventionally processed and partially recrystallized samples, with microstructural, tensile, fracture, and caloric measurements under identical conditions, can test the hypothesis.
The hypothesis is falsified if mechanical integrity does not improve significantly or if caloric performance decreases beyond experimental error.
